item.title: Design Engineering is the New Product Design
item.content:encoded:
\ A few weeks ago, I got challenged to figure out how the wave of new AI-powered tools (Figma Make, Codex, Antigravity, Claude) could actually fit into our existing workflows at work.

I should say: I already use these tools a lot on personal projects. (I post updates about these on X if you want to follow along) When it's just me, it's almost unfairly easy. No handoffs, no review cycles, no design system to stay consistent with. You just build. Something that would take a week of back-and-forth in a team setting takes an afternoon when you're solo.

But that's exactly the problem. Most of what gets written about AI and design is written from that solo perspective. And most of us aren't working solo.

I work at a Fortune 500 company. Large design org. Multiple product teams. Established engineering processes, compliance requirements, accessibility standards, a design system with hundreds of components. The kind of environment where a single change can have ripple effects across dozens of teams.

So the challenge wasn't "can AI tools help designers move faster." I already knew the answer to that. The real question was harder:

\

What does Design Engineering actually look like inside a large, complex organization and does it even work?

\

Where It All Started

It's worth going back a bit, because the current shift actually rhymes with something that happened before.

In the early days of software, developers built everything. The same person writing the code decided how the interface looked. UX wasn't a discipline, it was an afterthought embedded inside the build process.

Then the web grew up. Users started caring about more than just functionality. They wanted things that felt good, looked right, were actually usable. That's what opened the door for designers to step in.

I remember when I started out in India about a decade ago, knowing basic HTML was almost a prerequisite for getting a Product Design role. Companies were pulling in graphic designers and needed people who could at least speak the language of implementation. There was no clean separation yet.

Over time, the industry matured. Design tools got better. Teams grew. Dedicated Product Design roles became the norm, and the expectation that designers should code slowly faded. We got to focus on research, UX, visual design, systems. Each of those became its own sub-discipline.

But here's the thing. Looking at where we are now, it feels like the industry is coming full circle.

\

\

Why Things Are Moving Again

A few forces are colliding at once.

AI has dramatically lowered the cost of building. Tools can now generate interfaces, write frontend code, and scaffold entire prototypes in minutes. Work that once required a designer and an engineer can now be done by one person with the right workflow.

Design and code are also speaking the same language now. Design tokens, component libraries, shared systems these have been bridging the gap quietly for years. A recent signal of where this is heading: Google introduced the concept of the design.md file, a structured document that captures design principles, patterns, and implementation guidelines in a format that both humans and AI can read and act on. It sounds like a small thing, but it points at something much larger. Design intent is becoming something machines can interpret, not just designers.

The artifact of design is no longer just a Figma frame. It's a set of rules, constraints, and decisions that feed directly into how a product gets built.

What Design Engineering Actually Means

\

The term Design Engineering has been floating around for a while. But I want to be specific about what it means in practice, because a lot of people either overcompress or overcomplicate it.

It's not a designer who learned to code. It's not an engineer who has an eye for UI.

It's someone who operates at the intersection of both and uses that position to reduce the gap between a design decision and how it actually ships. Product thinking, UX principles, design systems knowledge, frontend skills, accessibility awareness all in one person, all reinforcing each other.

What makes this role compound over time is that every new skill strengthens the others. Learning a JS framework makes you a better prototyper. Understanding design systems makes your code more consistent. Working directly in components makes accessibility something you apply in context, not just audit after the fact.

AI accelerates all of it. But it doesn't replace any of it.

The Workflow That Actually Worked

I want to be honest about what I learned the hard way here.

The original goal was ambitious: use AI-assisted workflows to go from design concepts directly to production-ready output with minimal engineering involvement. In practice, that didn't fully work. In a large organization, you can't just generate interfaces and call it done. There are component governance processes, accessibility reviews, design system consistency to maintain, developer sign-off. The outputs were fast but they weren't ready for that environment.

What eventually worked was a different model entirely.

Instead of treating design as a separate phase that gets handed off, we brought designers into the development process itself. Storybook became the source of truth. Designers started updating components directly through code, using Figma MCP as a bridge. Motion, states, edge cases, interactions all validated inside the actual component environment, not just inside design files.

Design decisions got validated in realistic contexts. Components became production assets, not static mockups. When something was off, we could catch it, iterate, fix it, and move on without blowing up the handoff process or filing a ticket and waiting two sprints.

Engineers moved further into architecture and business logic. Designers got closer to the thing they'd always been trying to influence: the final product.

In a smaller team, this probably happens naturally. But at scale, with siloed teams and long feedback loops baked into the process, this kind of shift requires intentionality. It doesn't just happen.

Skills: The Part Nobody Talks About

\ This is where things got genuinely interesting for me.

Every step in our process that could be automated became what I'd call a skill, a small focused instruction set that tells the AI exactly what to do in a specific situation. Think of it like plugins in Figma, except you build them yourself, and each one is just a bunch of markdown files. No complicated setup. No proprietary format. No engineering dependency to ship something new. Just clear instructions that an AI agent can follow.

The reason this matters at scale: once you've defined a skill, that step of your workflow stops being manual across the entire team. You write it once, and it runs every time, for everyone.

Here's what that looked like in practice:

We had a Figma-to-Storybook skill. You paste a Figma URL, and it handles the translation, making sure all the variables, colors, and spacing are mapped to the right Storybook tokens or code connect references, not hardcoded values. In a large design system with hundreds of components, this kind of consistency check used to be a tedious manual process. Someone had to catch it in review. Now it's just caught.

\

We had a Code Connect skill that developers triggered when a component was approved. It would automatically wire up the Figma component to its Storybook counterpart, keeping design and code representations in sync without anyone having to manually maintain that mapping across the org.

There were others skills for checking accessibility on new components, skills for generating motion specs from interaction notes, skills for flagging when a component state was missing.

None of these required anyone to learn a new tool or sit through an onboarding. Each skill lived in the workspace, ready to be called whenever that step came up.

This is what I think is underrated about the Design Engineering shift, especially at the enterprise level. It's not just about designers writing more code. It's about designers being close enough to the process that they can define how parts of that process run. In an org where bottlenecks are everywhere and handoffs are slow, that's a different kind of leverage than we've had before.

Two Approaches That Are Emerging

In practice, I'm seeing two models take shape for how designers engage with this new world.

The first is prototype-first. Use AI tools, code generators, whatever gets a functional experience in front of someone quickly. In a large org, this is especially valuable because the feedback loops are long. Getting something in front of stakeholders or a developer team earlier, even if it's not production-ready compresses time and reduces misalignment before it becomes expensive.

The second is production-ready. Designers work inside design systems and component libraries. AI accelerates creation and iteration, but the output is something that can actually ship. This is where the real payoff is at scale, fewer handoff issues, better consistency across teams, less rework.

Neither is universally right. But in a big team, the prototype-first approach often clears the path for the production-ready work to go smoother. Both require designers to think about implementation, and that's the shift that matters.

What AI Still Can't Do (or still getting there)

Here's what I keep coming back to.

AI can generate an interface in minutes. What it can't do is know whether the information architecture is right for your users. Whether the interaction pattern makes sense in the context of your product ecosystem. Whether it's accessible across the range of users your company serves. Whether it will still make sense to a new designer who joins the team in eight months. That's still the job.

At a Fortune 500 scale, the stakes on these questions are higher. You're not just shipping to a small user base. Mistakes at this scale are expensive to fix. That's actually why design judgment matters more, not less, in this new world because the speed of production is going up, and someone still has to make sure the right things are getting built.

Does Every Designer on a Large Team Need to Do This?

Probably not.

Large orgs will always need specialists. Research, service design, accessibility, content design, design systems those are deep disciplines that reward focus. The industry isn't collapsing into one role, and it shouldn't.

But understanding implementation is becoming a real competitive advantage, even in big teams. Especially in big teams, actually because the designers who can sit in a sprint and contribute directly to a component, who can review a pull request and understand what they're looking at, who can build a skill that saves their whole team an hour a week, those designers have a different kind of influence than the ones handing off static screens and waiting.

If this feels overwhelming, Figma Make is a low-friction place to start. It sits inside a workflow most designers already know. Bring in your frames, generate interactive prototypes, start to see how design decisions translate into working interfaces. It's not really learning to code. It's learning to think a bit closer to the build.

https://x.com/zoink/status/2021045430952526275?embedable=true

What I Actually Took Away

When I started exploring all of this, I thought the lesson would be about AI. The real lesson was about proximity.

The closer you are to how something gets built, the easier it becomes to validate your decisions, catch the gaps, and ship something that actually reflects what you intended. In a large organization, that proximity is hard to get. There are layers between the design intent and the final product, and things get lost in those layers all the time.

Design Engineering, for me, was a way of closing some of those gaps. Not by becoming a developer. Not by taking over engineering. But by being close enough to the process that I could actually see where things were going wrong and do something about it.
